F-15.contradicts:
Checked every other place the document could already cover this, and one place the fix must deliberately NOT go.

(1) The document DOES set an explicit bar for a tenth SHOT — Global Constraints, lines 43-45, byte-exact: "- **Nine shots.** Every shot is a file that moves whenever `client/` changes or AlphaTab is upgraded.\n  A tenth must justify itself; if its stated coverage **is** a surface step, score that step against\n  the `1408.6` per-pixel cutoff before writing it." That bar is live and obeyed in-document: line 1414 declines a tenth shot by citing it ("Deliberately NOT a tenth shot: per Global Constraints a tenth must score its surface step against the 1408.6 cutoff"). No equivalent bar exists for a fifth ASSERTION. Confirmed by fixed-string sweep: `fifth` appears once in the whole document (line 564, about a `docker run` copy); `anchor`/`extend`/`in step`/`in lockstep` never appear in a sentence telling anyone to grow the guard's list.

(2) The nearest existing text is a REMOVAL rule, not an addition rule: Task 10 Step 3's runbook block ends "Do not remove one." (line 2159). It governs the opposite direction. No duplication.

(3) The parity assertion does not duplicate the guard's own trailing `assert.ok(sources.some((source) => source.includes('backgroundColor')), …)` at lines 1646-1648. That one fires only when EVERY surface assertion is gone; the parity assertion is strictly finer and fires on the first unanchored one. They compose.

(4) The fix deliberately does NOT add a Global Constraints bullet, even though that is where the tenth-shot bar lives. Global Constraints opens "Every task's requirements implicitly include this section. Values are copied verbatim from the spec." (lines 31) — a rule invented during implementation review is not a value copied from the spec, so putting it there would make that sentence false. It goes in the guard's own comment and the runbook instead, which is where a future contributor actually meets it.

(5) COMPANION EDITS the fix must carry, because the document's hard-coded counts are already drifting — which is the same defect class F-15 names, materialized: Task 8 Step 4's heading reads "Four separate checks" over SIX numbered arms (lines 1670-1681; the lap-2 additions were appended without touching the count), and Task 10 Step 3's runbook says "**Four shots assert a surface the comparator cannot see.**" (line 2156) where the plan's own helper doc-comment says "THREE of these shots guard a surface step … between them carrying FOUR such assertions" (lines 1244-1245) and the guard comment agrees, "Three shots carry four assertions" (line 1623). The `after` text corrects both.

No contradiction found. One genuine scope note: the finding as filed says a new assertion must score against the cutoff "the same way a tenth shot must", and the direction is the mirror — a tenth SHOT is scored to learn whether it can see its own subject, a fifth ASSERTION is scored to learn whether the picture already does. The `after` text states that explicitly rather than transplanting the sentence.

F-15.scenario: Months from now you add one more colour check to one of the pictures — the drop-zone panel, say — because the picture itself cannot tell that shade of grey from the page behind it. You write it exactly the way the four before it are written, every check goes green, and it merges. A year later someone tidying that file deletes your line. Every check stays green. The picture is byte-identical, because the picture never could see that shade in the first place — that is the whole reason you wrote the line. Nothing tells anybody. The state you added the check for is now unguarded, and the only trace is one missing line in a file nobody re-reads. Delete one of the four original checks instead and the build stops you by name in under a second, quoting which one you dropped.
F-15.whats_wrong: Task 8 Step 2's guard protects the four surface assertions by hard-coding them, one regex per assertion, in a fixed four-entry `[step, pattern]` array (lines 1635-1640). Nothing in the document tells a later contributor to extend that array, and nothing detects a new assertion that was never added to it. The result is a protection that applies to exactly today's four and to nothing added afterwards. The asymmetry is sharp because the document governs the OTHER growth axis carefully: Global Constraints sets a bar for a tenth shot (lines 43-45) and the plan cites that bar in-line when declining one (line 1414), while Task 10 Step 3's runbook says only "Do not remove one." (line 2159) — a removal rule, never an addition rule. Since every neutral surface step in this design system scores under the 1408.6 cutoff (5, 20, 80, 173), more assertions are the expected direction, not a hypothetical.
F-15.proposed_fix: Make the guard count its own anchors instead of only walking them, and say so in the two places a contributor reads. In Task 8 Step 2, hoist the four-entry `[step, pattern]` array into a named `surfaceAnchors` const and add one `assert.equal` above the loop comparing the number of surface assertions found in the shot sources to the number of anchors — so a fifth assertion without a fifth anchor fails at ADD time, not silently a year later at delete time. Add the growth rule to the guard's comment and to Task 10 Step 3's runbook block: a new computed background-color assertion scores its step against the 1408.6 cutoff first (above it the picture already covers it, so the assertion is noise; under it the assertion earns its place) and then adds its own anchor. Fix the two counts the fix touches — Step 4's "Four separate checks" heading, already stale over six arms, becomes seven with the new negative control, and the runbook's "Four shots" becomes "Three shots carry four assertions", which is what the plan's own helper comment and guard comment both already say.
F-15.why_it_works: Measured, not reasoned — the full four-cell matrix is in `spike`. The defect reproduced exactly: deleting a fifth surface assertion left the guard at `pass 1, fail 0` while the identical deletion of one of today's four gave `pass 0, fail 1` with `no *.vr.ts asserts the rail surface`, so the harness was provably live when it returned green. The doc-only fix as originally filed does work when obeyed (arm A went red on the deletion once the fifth anchor existed), but it is a soft obligation, and this document already contains a materialized instance of a soft obligation being skipped: Step 4's heading still reads "Four separate checks" over six arms because the lap-2 additions were appended without touching the count. The parity assertion removes the discipline entirely — it went red the moment a fifth assertion existed without an anchor, stayed green at 4/4 and at 5/5 so it is not permanently red, and went red again at 4/5 when the fifth was later dropped. The counting key was measured rather than assumed (exactly 2 then 3 helper-form matches, exactly 2 probe-form matches, no over-match anywhere in the document), and it stays helper-name-agnostic, which is the property the guard's own comment at line 1633 says the anchors deliberately preserve.

F-15.severity_rationale: P2 is right, and I would neither raise nor lower it. Not P1: nothing is broken the day this lands — all four assertions and all four anchors exist, every arm of the guard bites today, and the gap needs two future events to hurt anyone (a fifth assertion written, then dropped). Not P3: the guard's entire reason for existing, in its own words at line 1625, is that this class of loss is silent, and the spike showed the protection stopping dead at exactly today's four while the expected direction of travel is more assertions, since every neutral surface step in this design system already scores under the cutoff. The fix is cheap — one hoisted const, one `assert.equal`, one negative control, two prose sentences, and it corrects two counts that are already stale. It should land with this plan rather than become a follow-up, because after the plan ships nobody re-reads it.
